items.title: All The Things You’re Not Allowed To Say In Texas
items.description: S ara Spurgeon , an English professor at Texas Tech University in Lubbock, has been teaching literature for 20 years. But May 2025 was the first time she was forced to submit her course materials through a portal to be evaluated by an artificial-intelligence program. It flags anything that might violate new rules laid out by the university chancellor, including a prohibition on the “advocacy/promotion of race or sex-based prejudice,” and a requirement—now Texas state law—that “only two sexes, male and female, are recognized.” At Texas Tech, medical students no longer learn about racial disparities in medical care. Faculty at the university’s medical center in Lubbock were advised to “refrain from treating transgender patients, for any medical condition, if a medical student was present,” according to a lawsuit filed by the American Association of University Professors. (When asked for comment, a spokesperson said that the university’s “written guidance is publicly available and expressly protects instruction necessary for licensure and patient care.”) According to the same lawsuit, the censorship bot—officially known as the Course Content Review Process—ordered a Tech philosophy professor to remove Plato’s Republic from a syllabus because “it references Plato’s beliefs concerning gender roles and homosexuality.” Professors in the Texas A&M system have had to strip their syllabi too. According to an ACLU lawsuit , last January, Aaron George, a professor at Tarleton State University, was told by administrators to remove A Gay Manifesto , a Stonewall-era LGBTQ-rights pamphlet, and White Flight , a history of urban segregation, from his American-political-history course. After a student complained that a different class the professor taught violated university policy, George was informed by administrators that it would be canceled if he did not make “necessary” (but unspecified) changes. He cut a reference in the course description to the significance of the Fourteenth Amendment for LGBTQ rights, and the class was allowed to proceed. The University of Texas at Austin, the flagship school of the UT system, announced last month that it was eliminating majors in Africana studies, Mexican American and Latino studies, women’s and gender studies, and race and migration studies. More than 100 courses have been flagged for removal from the core curriculum, primarily ones relating to slavery, race, gender, sexuality, and the environment. Consolidating majors isn’t necessarily nefarious, nor is rethinking a core curriculum (a central group of courses from which students must take a certain number to graduate). But these changes are happening, Lauren Gutterman, an American studies professor at UT, told me, “entirely because of the political context.” [ Adam Kirsch: Texas sends Plato back to his cave ] The changes to Texas public-university systems are being presented as a necessary corrective to left-wing orthodoxy on campus. Over the past decade, many Americans have come to believe that academia is too ideological and too intolerant of conservative views and arguments. Censoriousness is not an exclusively left-wing phenomenon, but it is real. And some conservative speakers on college campuses met with protests that, while themselves a form of speech, occasionally deteriorated into violence . “Our nation is witnessing a merciless campaign to wipe out our history, defame our heroes, erase our values, and indoctrinate our children,” President Trump declared in 2019 . “One of their political weapons is ‘Cancel Culture’—driving people from their jobs, shaming dissenters, and demanding total submission from anyone who disagrees. This is the very definition of totalitarianism, and it is completely alien to our culture and our values.” Perhaps it’s less alien than Trump supposed. In the name of fighting propaganda and indoctrination, Texan politicians have established strict state controls on what can be taught, researched, and even discussed in the classroom. However bad left-wing censoriousness is or was, the Republican response in Texas has been to ensure that what is taught in the state’s universities is itself propaganda and indoctrination. Ellen Schrecker, a historian of McCarthyism at Yeshiva University, told me that this campaign goes beyond even the repression of the McCarthy era, when censorship led to firings and purges but the government did not interfere directly with what students were taught. After all, American politicians understood that there was a Cold War to win, and that it could not be won if the universities themselves were destroyed. By outlawing or banning forms of speech and inquiry, and by eliminating faculty independence, today’s Republicans are doing much more damage. Texas passed the first of its education gag laws in 2021 to limit the teaching of “critical race theory” in K–12 classrooms. Texas also tried to ban books dealing with racism or LGBTQ themes from public and school libraries; lawmakers characterized the latter as “pornography.” In 2023, the legislature banned “diversity, equity, and inclusion” in higher education, leading to the closure of DEI offices at state-funded institutions. Last year, Texas passed Senate Bill 37 to sharply curtail shared governance—the process by which faculty, administrators, and boards collaborate in running universities; this left political appointees and administrators with unchecked power over hiring and curricula. Governor Greg Abbott had bragged about signing a free-speech law in 2019. Following pro-Palestinian protests on Texas campuses in 2023, he signed a new law banning “expressive activities” from 10 p.m. to 8 a.m., and allowing schools to forbid student protests in some public areas. The seven Texas public-university systems serve more than 700,000 students—several times the enrollment of all Ivy League institutions combined. There are many ways to destroy a university. Texas Tech, Texas A&M, and the University of Texas have each taken a different approach to enforcing the new state laws, with varying degrees of heavy-handedness. But the result will be the same: substandard education, substandard research, and graduates who are less prepared for their future as workers, thinkers, and citizens, and more prepared to obey without question. T exas Tech’s approach to censorship is notable for being both onerous and clumsy, in part because it relies so heavily on artificial intelligence. Curriculum review traditionally involved faculty, administrators, department chairs, and deans who offered expert input without subjecting teaching decisions to the whims of trustees or politicians who might have political or economic interests in avoiding certain subjects. The process still involves layers of review from administrators and university leaders, but the faculty’s role has been replaced in part by the censorship bot, which scans course materials considered potentially controversial. Asked about the role of AI, a spokesperson for the university said that “the Course Content Review process will continue to be faculty-led, just as it was designed to be from the beginning.” Texas Tech’s new chancellor, Brandon Creighton, is a former Texas legislator and the author of Senate Bill 37, the law that limited shared governance . Creighton said he intended for the bill to “eliminate woke indoctrination in core courses” and give “Texans the power to report biased or inappropriate instruction.” The original text contained explicit “identity politics” restrictions that were stripped from the final version, possibly because they might not have passed legal muster. The policy he has implemented at Texas Tech, however, resembles the original version. Creighton has said he believes that it will be a “national model.” Creighton issued two memos outlining the restrictions, including one threatening faculty members that a failure to report any course content “implicated” by the policy would result in “disciplinary action.” Another announced a phaseout of all degree programs related to what the memo referred to as SOGI (“Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity”). It also formalizes a ban on “instruction that advocates for concepts of inherent racial or sexual superiority, inherent bias, or collective guilt.” In the future, the memo states, no degree “will be permitted to center on SOGI topics.” Such a ban on entire fields of study, inquiry, and discourse, Creighton said—preposterously—would foster “diversity of viewpoint.” For many years, Sara Spurgeon has taught a literature class focused on social justice and the environment. She has often assigned Ta-Nehisi Coates’s Pulitzer Prize–winning memoir Between the World and Me , but this time, the book was flagged by the bot as promoting “the belief that meritocracy is a construct of oppression designed to exploit Black bodies,” and it therefore “directly violates the system’s Prohibition of Prejudiced Advocacy.” (The word meritocracy does not appear in the book.) Creighton has insisted that “studying Black history, discussing the realities of racism, and treating every student with respect are not prohibited.” Spurgeon told me that works by science fiction and fantasy authors were also flagged. In other professors’ syllabi, the bot flagged the Pulitzer Prize–winning play Angels in America by Tony Kushner, essays by the Mexican American MacArthur genius grant recipient Sandra Cisneros, and materials related to a class about the Holocaust (that professor was told to drop material regarding Nazi persecution of LGBTQ people). Putting aside the ideological slant of the new rules, the bot, like many large language models, seems to “hallucinate,” or make mistakes. The AAUP lawsuit lists texts banned for their “sex-based ecofeminist framework” and “gendered ecofeminist frameworks.” These phrases might sound persuasively like academese, but the academics behind the lawsuit had never heard of them; these concepts “do not exist,” the complaint says. Matthew Pehl, a history professor at Tech, told me that he knew several people who’d received reports from the system that were “plainly written by an AI that had hallucinated content or confused content from one class to another.” Alan Barenberg, a history professor who specializes in the Soviet Union, was told to remove readings by the Princeton historian Joan Scott and the French philosopher Michel Foucault from his Ph.D.-level historiography class, after they were flagged by the AI—whose assessments he described to me as “completely inaccurate.” It also seemed to have mixed his course up with a different one. The texts were part of a unit of the class related to how treatment of gender in historical research has changed over time. “These things have been taught in classes for a long time,” Barenberg told me. The material is controversial, he said, only “in the eyes of a few people who aren’t even actually on campus.” “The fact that the system AI doesn’t work, that it makes inaccurate pronouncements—that’s a feature, not a bug. They don’t care if it’s accurate or not. They just want to be able to say, Look, we’re making sure that your children are not being exposed to these horrible ideas from these radical professors ,” Barenberg said. “A key part of how authoritarian systems often work is that, through the vagueness and sending up signals and vibes, they’re essentially saying, You know what not to do , but being deliberately vague about it.” Although the AI is now reviewing only some courses, the university could extend the process to more. For now, professors are the ones responsible for volunteering whether their own materials may be considered controversial. Many, unsure of what might trigger the bot, told me that they had private conversations with administrators who told them to simply self-censor and remove materials from their courses in advance, so as not to draw the wrath of leadership or lawmakers. Pehl, the history professor, told me that he did just that, and decided not to use the book Scraping By , about labor in Revolutionary-era Baltimore, because he had been planning on teaching it early in the year, which didn’t allow time for it to be reviewed first. The book differentiates between the experiences of workers based on whether they were enslaved or free, men or women. William Wenthe, a poetry professor, didn’t mark his course as potentially controversial, though he told me that he was worried: He teaches T. S. Eliot’s The Wasteland , which includes a male character from Greek mythology who becomes a woman. Could a Texan politician object to that? Censorship infantilizes students, he said: “They’re old enough to vote. They’re all old enough to fight and die for this country. And you’re treating them like babies.” Texas Tech’s censorship policy does not just affect the humanities. According to the AAUP lawsuit, medical students at the campus in El Paso are no longer permitted to learn about racial disparities in medical care or how to treat underserved populations—both major challenges in the overwhelmingly Hispanic Texas border region. At the Lubbock campus, a professor of health sciences at the medical school was told that he could not teach about transgender or intersex patients. Some professors are leaving. Breanna Harris told me she quit her job as a biology professor at the Lubbock campus in part because she says administrators informed her that she could not use the American Medical Association’s definitions of sex and gender , which, by distinguishing between the two, run afoul of Texas law. Harris’s course materials, she said, ask questions such as “How do organisms become ‘male’ or ‘female’?” and “What does that process look like biologically during development?” Lisa Limeri, a biology professor at Texas Tech who had just been awarded tenure this year, resigned for the same reason. “We are not allowed to teach topics that are relevant to things like the MCAT and being practicing medical professionals,” she told me. “We are not allowed to teach them scientifically, accurately.” A spokesperson for the university pushed back on the claim that medical students were not being taught what they would need to do their jobs: “We have tremendous confidence in our faculty and their commitment to preparing students to provide excellent care. It is important to distinguish between what our policy actually requires and restrictions that are not found anywhere in our written guidance.” According to an internal survey, more than half of Tech’s faculty are looking for work elsewhere. In a private meeting with faculty, a recording of which was shared with me, a provost acknowledged that “on average, we have 20 percent to 25 percent fewer people applying for jobs here.” When professors challenged him on why he was not fighting against censorship, the provost said he couldn’t stop it: “It’s going to happen. And so you can try to help slow or mitigate it,” he said. “Or you can bring in people who will help it happen faster. That’s the option at the moment.” Texas Tech is an R1 research university, which means that it receives a large amount of federal funding to produce significant amounts of research. But the censorship policy leaves entire fields of scientific inquiry banned, even for Ph.D. students. “America has risen to global prominence in science and scientific research because of the strength of our system,” Limeri said. “If these kinds of censorship policies were implemented everywhere, we would have a generation of students who are not learning to think critically, are not learning to think for themselves, and are not learning full and accurate scientific information.” Administrators told faculty in that private meeting not to discuss the censorship policy with students, because it might generate “a lot of fear and a lot of anger and anxiety.” T he Texas A&M system , which serves about 175,000 students, doesn’t have an AI censor. But it does have both a strict, arbitrary, and confusing censorship policy and elected leaders joining online mobs against professors. Melissa McCoul, a senior lecturer in the English department at Texas A&M’s College Station campus, has taught her course on children’s literature 11 times since arriving at the university in 2017. And she would have continued to do so, if Governor Abbott hadn’t demanded she be fired. In July 2025, Brian Harrison, a Republican state representative, reposted a slide from McCoul’s class that had been highlighted by another X user. The slide argued that queerness can be discussed in “age-appropriate” terms and that homosexuality was not an “x-rated” concept. Harrison declared that “Texans are being taxed out of their homes to fund liberal indoctrination.” McCoul immediately found herself at the mercy of a social-media mob. A little more than two weeks later, a student interrupted McCoul’s class to say that her teachings were “against the law.” After a brief exchange, McCoul asked the student to leave. In September (by which time McCoul was teaching a different class), Harrison posted a video of the summer confrontation and described the student as “OBJECTING TO TRANSGENDER INDOCTRINATION.” Harrison also posted a letter he had sent to Abbott reminding him that “during your State of the State Address, you stated that ‘any educator who tells students that boys can be girls should be fired on the spot.’” Mark Welsh, then the president of A&M, replied to Harrison’s post with a statement that the class had been canceled and that “key leaders” had been removed for allowing McCoul to teach “course content that was not consistent with the course’s published description.” Abbott joined the mob, replying, “Good. Now, fire the professor who acted contrary to Texas law.” Promptly, the university did. McCoul claims that the course never deviated from the catalog description and has sued the university for ignoring its own due-process procedures; the lawsuit is ongoing. According to her complaint, two faculty panels reviewing the incident found no good cause for her firing. Welsh has since resigned. In a motion to dismiss McCoul’s suit, filed in April, A&M states that McCoul was an untenured senior lecturer and that “Texas A&M University is entitled to state sovereign immunity as an ‘arm of the state.’” The motion also argues that “the termination was lawful and was certainly no violation of the lecturer’s academic freedom or the First Amendment.” The university alleges that McCoul “used the class as an opportunity to indoctrinate her students into transgender and LGBTQ ideology,” and that “by kicking out a student” who expressed a contrary opinion and “threatening” to kick out others, McCoul “interfered with those students’ academic freedom.” The filing also makes sure to point out that “she began the class by introducing herself as an autistic lesbian.” In December, A&M adopted a policy stating that “no system academic course will advocate race or gender ideology, or topics related to sexual orientation or gender identity.” The next month, the women’s and gender studies programs were eliminated. The policy defines gender ideology as the idea “that self-assessed gender identity should replace the biological category of sex,” whereas race ideology “attempts to shame a particular race or ethnicity, accuse them of being oppressors in a racial hierarchy or conspiracy, ascribe to them less value as contributors to society and public discourse because of their race or ethnicity, or assign them intrinsic guilt based on the actions of their presumed ancestors.” If a professor acknowledges the existence of trans people, they could be violating the first policy; if they describe race-based chattel slavery in the antebellum United States, they could be violating the second. Their livelihood might depend on how much time the governor of Texas is spending on social media that day. Leonard Bright, a tenured professor at A&M’s Bush School of Government and Public Service, is one of several other professors suing the university for its censorship policy. This year, his graduate-level course on ethics and public policy was canceled. His lawsuit says that he informed the administration that “at no point does the course require students to adopt, affirm, or reject particular beliefs regarding these topics. Students are evaluated solely on analytical rigor, use of evidence, and professional engagement.” Still, he told me, the university wouldn’t approve the class unless he provided “a detailed day-by-day description of when sexual orientation is going to come up.” And he couldn’t do that, because “this is a discussion course.” The policy raises other uncomfortable questions for Prairie View A&M, a historically Black college in the A&M system that was first established by the Reconstruction-era legislature as a segregated institution . There’s no way to even explain its existence without touching on matters that could be caricatured as “race ideology.” The difference between “advocating” and “teaching” is not clearly defined, but the way the censorship policy is being implemented makes the situation pretty clear: If you’re using material that state lawmakers agree with, that’s teaching; if you’re talking about something they object to, that’s advocacy, and you have to stop. As detailed in a complaint against Texas A&M filed by the ACLU, an English professor, Vanita Reddy, was told that the censorship policy “will not be applied to heteronormative orientation and identity,” but exclusively to “LGBTQ gender identity or sexual orientation.” George, the history professor who was told to remove several texts perceived as liberal, was allowed to teach the conservative anti-feminist activist Phyllis Schlafly’s “What’s Wrong With Equal Rights for Women?” P rofessors at UT Austin aren’t seeing their classes summarily canceled or scrubbed for forbidden terms by a censorship AI. They haven’t been told to list the dates that gender might come up. The governor hasn’t demanded the heads of any of its professors. “Gender and race ideology” have not been banned. While Texas Tech and Texas A&M received an “F” from the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, a free-speech watchdog, UT Austin earned a “D–”. What UT has done is issue a statement on “academic integrity” urging professors to “fairly present differing views and scholarly evidence on reasonably disputed matters and unsettled issues” and “to eschew topics and controversies that are not germane to the course.” No one is really sure what that means—and that may be the point. “Nobody yet has been disciplined under this policy,” Julie Minich, an English professor who focuses on Latino literature, told me. “But also, nobody wants to be the first one to be disciplined under the policy.” The university did not respond to repeated requests by phone and email to speak about this story or to a list of questions. [ Adam Serwer: Speak at your own risk ] Peter Onyisi, a physics professor, has for years used the greenhouse effect as an example of a real-world, practical effect of quantum mechanics to students. Although he does not plan to stop, he worries that administrators could argue that climate change is not “germane” to his course. But that’s not how teaching works, Onyisi pointed out: “You can’t really say, Oh, physics is in a nice little box, and it doesn’t talk to anything else .” Academic freedom is under assault in the UT system, he said, just in more “subtle” ways than elsewhere. Jim Davis, the president of UT, has justified the cuts to the core curriculum by arguing that too many courses were “ narrow .” One of Davis’s favorite examples is a class on the history of college football, although, as one professor pointed out to me, the origins of the sport offer a fascinating view into the post–Civil War economy and culture of the South, not to mention a billion-dollar industry that is a big deal at, well, UT. That’s the thing about academic inquiry: Many seemingly “narrow” questions open up much bigger ones. Davis’s example, however, may be misleading. Given that most of the courses being targeted involve the study of gender or race, “narrow” seems to refer mainly to the study of people, subjects, or works that some conservatives consider unimportant. These sweeping changes couldn’t have happened “if shared governance was still in existence,” Lauren Gutterman, the American-studies professor, told me. “S.B. 37 has changed things dramatically in just a very short period of time.” A university task force has proposed that the new core include a “Great Questions of Human Life” requirement based on texts from preapproved “great thinkers.” A preliminary list of 50 names was sent out to faculty. The list includes three Black writers (W. E. B. Du Bois, Frederick Douglass, and Toni Morrison), six women (in addition to Morrison: Mary Shelley, Simone de Beauvoir, Mary Ann Evans, Jane Austen, and Mary Wollstonecraft), and no Hispanic or Latin American authors. The only Asian author on the list is Confucius. (UT has said it “intends” to expand the list ). A “Masterworks of Literature” requirement would pull most of its readings from the same list, and divide them into the categories “American,” “British,” and “World.” The proposed “Principles of American Politics” requirement warns that the courses should “focus on issues that involve the whole country, not just one region or group.” And under its “Western Civilization” requirement, the task force observes that “Western Civilization has interacted in complex ways with other civilizations”—middle-school writing that raises the question of what counts as Western civilization , a term that the report acknowledges it cannot define. “They’re saying that they need to be broad classes that satisfy the core requirements, not narrow classes,” Minich told me. But the effect is the opposite. “Rather than having a core curriculum that reflects the diversity of the campus in the public flagship of the second-most diverse state in the country, they’re moving toward a curriculum that is much more heavily focused on the European intellectual tradition. And they are calling that ‘breadth’ and saying that courses that fall outside that intellectual tradition are ‘narrow.’” Classes that get stripped of their core designation may end up scrapped altogether, because students have limited time. Declining enrollment in non-core classes can then be an excuse to dispose of them entirely. “At the time I came here, UT was the No. 1 place to do what I do—studying Latino literature. We have this long, rich history of Latino studies,” Minich said. “I see this as a first step toward eliminating an area of study that has been historically extremely important at this university.” In July, Iván Chaar López, an expert in the history of the U.S. southern border, was denied tenure , as Inside Higher Ed reported, despite the College of Liberal Arts tenure committee voting overwhelmingly in his favor. Chaar López told me that, in a meeting with administrators that February, he was told that the president’s tenure committee “had a negative view” of his work. He is challenging the decision, and is one of several faculty members or administrators who believe that they were fired, laid off, or denied tenure because their politics were seen as left-wing or because their expertise is among the subjects the administration has turned against. “It is almost as if we are meant to teach whatever fits into a political pamphlet. But that’s not what free inquiry and free speech and academic freedom are about,” Chaar López told me. Students are getting “an education that is all about obeying.” Angela Valenzuela, a professor in the department of educational leadership and policy, said that you should not be able to “graduate from UT Austin and not know anything about anything south of the Rio Grande River and call yourself an educated person.” She added, “This is not an argument about whether or not ‘Western civilization’ should be taught. It’s an argument of whether that’s what should be exclusively taught.” UT’s quiet restructuring of the university may prove to be more effective and sustainable than the tactics at Texas Tech and Texas A&M; UT’s censorship attempts, notably, have yet to face a legal challenge. Nonetheless, professors fear that the changes will leave students without the cognitive tools or contextual information to question matters that some conservatives would prefer not be questioned. Meanwhile, resources have been directed instead toward UT Austin’s new School of Civic Leadership, which claims to promote “freedom of thought and speech.” J en Shelton , an English professor at Texas Tech, told me that her daughter had gone to college in Minnesota. “When she had her first class,” Shelton said, “she called me to say, ‘You won’t believe all the things people are allowed to say up here.’” Some conservative activists have gone beyond attacking teachers. Brian Harrison, who led the campaign against the A&M professor, railed in September against the existence of an archive of LGBTQ-history primary-source documents at the University of North Texas. The webpage describing the archive was taken down; one begins to wonder whether the state will demand the destruction of the documents themselves next. In a 2026 AAUP survey , 70 percent of Texas faculty would not recommend taking a faculty position in the state, and about 30 percent said they had experienced censorship of courses by administrators. Texas “is on the leading edge” in the field of censorship in higher education, Jonathan Friedman, who directs PEN America’s work on free expression in the United States, told me. But Texas is hardly alone. According to PEN, Alabama, Florida, Indiana, and Utah have all adopted laws that seek to limit what professors are allowed to teach and what students are allowed to study. “Notions like academic freedom and free speech on campus are all just going out the window,” Friedman said. More Republican-leaning states will likely follow. Over the past decade, some conservatives have invoked principles of academic freedom and free speech in order to subvert both. These conservatives mocked “snowflakes” and “trigger warnings,” and then passed legislation making it illegal to hurt white students’ feelings by discussing historical or contemporary events. They invoked academic freedom and then began erasing fields of study they found politically inconvenient. They railed against “indoctrination,” and then argued that the state is entitled to control everything said in the classroom. [ Kevin Carey: The logical end point of Trump’s higher-education agenda ] One might argue that progressive influence on campus had gone too far and states needed to reestablish free-speech norms eroded during the zenith of the first anti-Trump backlash. Conservative ideas do have an important place in higher education—a well-rounded education is impossible otherwise. But there is a distinction between left-wing censoriousness and actual state censorship. Todd Wolfson, the president of AAUP, told me that he would be “the first to admit” that he witnessed people and ideas being “shut down from discussion” on campus. But, he said, “there’s no comparison in the ability and attempt to dictate ideas. Just none. One was informal, and the other is now formal and legal.” He continued, “I think it’s a fantasy to say that what happened then has any relationship to the extremism that we’re seeing right now.” The right-wing assault on higher education may be rooted in college-educated voters’ shift to the left. If one blames that shift on left-wing professors, then purging them from academia could change the way educated people vote. But educational polarization is a global phenomenon, and evidence shows that college does not alter students’ political beliefs as much as people assume. Attacking universities is more likely to simply degrade the quality of education than it is to help Republicans at the polls. Besides, in Texas, many students arrive as conservatives and stay that way. Many students have protested the new censorship policies, while others have enforced them, as demonstrated by the undergraduates turning their professors in for violations. University leaders have occasionally attempted to disguise their campaigns as an effort to better prepare Texas students for the workforce. Texas Tech Chancellor Brandon Creighton said that there was “quite a bit of garbage in curriculum all over university campuses all across America,” and that Tech would “remain the tip of the spear on producing the highest degree of value.” But the value of even the hardest STEM degree will be degraded if courses in those fields are censored for being politically inconvenient. And regardless, the quality of an education is not determined by the wealth you subsequently accumulate. So what can be done? Legal precedent seems to be on the side of people challenging the censorship policies, at least at Tech and A&M. The Supreme Court has held that academic freedom is a “special concern” that is “of transcendent value to all of us.” Florida, during litigation over the Stop WOKE Act, a similar ban on “divisive concepts,” tried to argue that the First Amendment didn’t apply to professors at state schools, because they were government employees. The Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals rejected that argument , concluding that “if the history of that Amendment tells us anything, it is that the government cannot forbid what it perceives as heresy.” The current right-wing majority on the Supreme Court, however, has shown itself willing to ignore the plain text of the Constitution where the latest culture-war fixation is concerned. “You have to go back to the loyalty oath cases of the Cold War period to see relatively analogous situations where the government was trying to silence academics with viewpoints that they didn’t like,” Emerson Sykes, an attorney with the ACLU, told me. “But even in those cases, we did not see the sort of brazen attempt to ban particular ideas or ideologies and scrub them from the public record or from public education.” Sykes cautioned me that although academic freedom interacts with the First Amendment, they are not synonymous. The Eleventh Circuit ruling found that state governments can “make ordinary curriculum decisions (like which majors or courses to offer), or otherwise ensure competent academic instruction.” For that reason, UT Austin’s structural changes are likely more resistant to legal challenge. Those who wish to oppose them may have to find other means, such as labor organizing or politics. That will be a monumental task—especially as universities are relying more and more on tenuously employed adjunct professors. In the meantime, the Trump administration has been meddling in higher education at the federal level—using grants to pressure universities into changing whom they admit and what they teach and research, and going after foreign students for their politics. The degradation of free speech doesn’t stop in Texas. And it won’t stay on campus either.

items.title: Comment lutter contre la tuberculose de l’olivier signalée à Mahdia et Sfax
items.description: Le Dr Noureddine Nasr, consultant international en développement agricole, a affirmé que la tuberculose de l’olivier, qui a fait l’objet récemment d’alertes phytosanitaires importantes dans les gouvernorats de Mahdia et de Sfax, n’est pas une maladie nouvelle, contrairement à ce qui est affirmé par certains sur les réseaux sociaux, précisant qu’il s’agit d’une maladie bactérienne connue de longue date dans le bassin méditerranéen. Cette maladie causée par la bactérie Pseudomonas savastanoi n’a aucun lien, non plus, avec la cochenille du cactus, qui a ravagé des milliers d’hectares de figues de Barbarie ces dernières années en Tunisie, a-t-il ajouté, lors de son intervention sur la radio Diwan FM, ce dimanche 11 octobre 2026. La bactérie responsable de la maladie est associée aux oliviers et est présente dans plusieurs pays méditerranéens, notamment la Tunisie, la Grèce, l’Italie et la France, a-t-il encore précisé, soulignant que l’infection peut affecter la productivité des arbres. L’expert international a appelé les agriculteurs à respecter un ensemble de mesures préventives pour protéger les oliveraies et limiter la propagation de l’infection entre les arbres, soulignant l’importance d’une intervention précoce et de l’adoption de pratiques agricoles saines. Dans ce contexte, il a insisté sur la nécessité d’éviter l’achat et la plantation de vieux oliviers déracinés — connus localement sous le nom de «Zitoun El Koub» — signalant que le transfert d’arbres infectés peut contribuer à la propagation de la bactérie vers d’autres arbres dans d’autres. Dr Nasr a également recommandé de s’approvisionner en plants exclusivement auprès de pépinières agréées et contrôlées par le ministère de l’Agriculture, tout en vérifiant les documents officiels et en évitant de traiter avec des pépinières informelles ou non autorisées. Il a, ensuite, mis en garde contre les risques de transmission de la bactérie par le biais des outils de taille, préconisant d’attribuer des outils spécifiques à chaque ouvrier et de les désinfecter conformément aux recommandations techniques en vigueur. Il a également conseillé de commencer par tailler les arbres sains avant de passer à ceux suspectés d’être infectés ou déjà atteints, tout en recommandant de retirer les branches et les chancres infectés et de les traiter selon les directives phytosanitaires officielles, en les brûlant immédiatement sur place, au pied de l’arbre, tout en évitant de les transporter sans précaution d’un champ à l’autre, afin de limiter les risques de propagation de l'infection. Il convient, par ailleurs, de prêter attention au rôle de certains insectes dans la transmission de la bactérie, sachant que la rapidité de propagation de la maladie exige vigilance, suivi périodique de l’état des arbres et intervention dès l’apparition des symptômes. Ces recommandations s’inscrivent dans le cadre d’un appel à renforcer la prévention et à protéger la récolte d’olives en Tunisie, en sensibilisant les agriculteurs aux modes de transmission de la maladie et en adoptant des méthodes de lutte fondées sur des directives techniques spécialisées. I. B. L’article Comment lutter contre la tuberculose de l’olivier signalée à Mahdia et Sfax est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: 'No lesson learnt': KP emergency evokes grim October memories
items.description: Sunday, Oct 11, evoked grim memories for many in Pakistan, as the federal government imposed emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The cabinet was certain of the decision, but many others warned against repeating what they saw as an “ill-advised step”. Nevertheless, it happened, again. The threat of emergency and governor’s rule had been looming over the province for days, after the PTI announced its long march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. It materialised on Sunday. It began with a federal cabinet meeting where Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif was briefed on the security situation in KP, which the Centre had earlier been linking with the need for emergency in the province. The cabinet reviewed the situation, took note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”, and gave the nod to impose emergency and governor’s rule in KP. A signature by President Asif Ali Zardari, and the decision was implemented shortly after. The development took veteran journalist Mazhar Abbas on a trip down memory lane, apparently a grim one. “Why [does] October often bring ‘bad news’ for democracy from 1958 to 2026?” he posted on X. “Saddest part is that each time one party or the other welcomed such moves. On Oct 12, 1999 when PM Nawaz was sacked, the PPP welcomed the move. Now, the PPP and PML-N agreed to get rid of the PTI KP government. No lesson learnt,” he lamented. Former ambassador and analyst Maleeha Lodhi agreed. “Really nothing learnt from history,” she too posted, replying to Abbas’s comment. Analyst Niaz Murtaza was more thorough in recounting the historical trend of what Abbas described as “bad news” from October. “October is perhaps the worst month for democracy,” Murtaza commented, sharing a list of instances from history: On the latest imposition of emergency in KP, he said the move was “deeply condemnable, unfortunate and ill-advised”. “The clearly illegitimate nature of the central government makes it doubly so. This could make the situation in KP much more complicated,” he warned. Others, too, warned against the move and its consequences. Among them was National Democratic Movement Chairperson Bushra Gohar, who posted a warning the night before emergency was imposed. “Emergency will further aggravate the already volatile political and security situation in Pakhtunkhwa. The province cannot afford yet another failed experiment after the disastrous pro-Taliban TTPTI government — 13 years of incompetence, loot and plunder, death and devastation,” she posted on X on the night before emergency was imposed. Instead, she added, free, fair and credible elections were the only way forward. Similarly, the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan cautioned the federal government and Parliament in a statement that declaring emergency or imposing governor’s rule in KP risked further deepening of political tensions and undermining of democratic processes. “We strongly urge the federal government and the PTI to resume a meaningful political dialogue immediately and ensure that citizens’ fundamental rights are not suspended under any pretext,” the statement said. Lawyer Rida Hosain pointed to the potential implication of emergency particularly for former tribal areas. She noted in a post on X that the imposition of emergency allowed the executive to suspend certain fundamental rights. “To impose emergency rule over the former tribal areas is to push the people of those areas back into a legal black hole where their fundamental rights are treated as dispensable,” she said. Journalist Ihsanullah Tipu Mehsud saw emergency as a move that “frees the PTI” and “traps the Centre”. Because “Islamabad owns security, PTI owns the narrative,” he explained on X. Former IT minister Umar Saif explained Mehsud’s deduction in more detail, saying that imposing emergency in KP “comes with an enormous burden of responsibility”. “It is not merely an exercise of authority; it is a commitment to fix what has gone wrong. The government must now deliver. Failure will deepen public disillusionment, hand fresh ammunition to the naysayers, and discredit the very idea of reform. “Reform demands clarity of intent, consistency of purpose, and the resolve to see it through. We have seen too many initiatives falter midway, leaving behind resentment and eroding faith in the process,” he said. Meanwhile, journalist Shahzad Iqbal noted that PPP Chairperson Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari had called emergency a “political atomic bomb”. “Yet President Zardari has completed hat-trick of imposing governor’s rule,” he said, recounting the previous two instances — in 2009 in Punjab and in 2013 in Balochistan. “The irony is hard to miss,” he commented. Header image: A general view shows a road blocked with shipping containers amid ongoing protests by the PTI party demanding the release of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan in Peshawar on October 11, 2026. — AFP

items.title: Intercity transport suspended in Lahore, bus terminals reportedly sealed
items.description: LAHORE: Intercity bus services from Lahore to several destinations across the country were suspended on Sunday after the administration reportedly sealed all general bus terminals in the city late on Saturday night, leaving passengers stranded and disrupting travel. The closures affected passengers travelling to Islamabad, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Sindh, southern Punjab and other parts of central Punjab. Several passengers reported difficulties after their tickets were cancelled and transport services suspended. Meanwhile, major private bus operators, including Faisal Movers and Daewoo, suspended their services amid reports of restrictions on public transport movement on motorways and national highways. Representatives of Faisal Movers and Daewoo told Dawn that their services had been suspended and buses were not being dispatched due to the restrictions. However, motorway police spokesperson Imran Shah told Dawn that motorways and highways were open to traffic and that he was unaware of any directions to suspend bus services. Another motorway police official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said buses were not operating on motorways or highways because of the PTI’s protest call. He added that people travelling in private vehicles could use the roads. Punjab Transport Department Secretary Imran Sikandar Baloch was unavailable for comment despite repeated attempts to contact him on his mobile phone. The development comes as the PTI launched its march on October 4 despite warnings from the Centre. So far, the march — being carried out to demand Imran’s release — has remained within KP, where the PTI is in power. A day earlier, containers were transported to Swabi Interchange — where the PTI had called on its workers to gather — as well as the Indus River bridge on the M-1 Motorway to block the party’s march, but the motorway and the Grand Trunk Road remain open to traffic.

items.title: Drame conjugal a Sénégal : Cheikhou Oumar Ndiaye poignardé à mort dans son sommeil par sa seconde épouse
items.description: Dans la nuit du jeudi 8 au vendredi 9 octobre 2026, le paisible village de Sam Ndiaye, situé dans la commune de Fandène, a été le théâtre d'un homicide conjugal d'une rare violence. Cheikhou Oumar Ndiaye, un chauffeur et cultivateur d'une quarantaine d'années, a été poignardé à mort dans son sommeil par sa seconde épouse, Asta Dia, sur fond de différend familial. Mortellement touché de deux coups de couteau, ce père de six enfants s'est effondré après avoir désigné son agressrice dans un dernier souffle, laissant une communauté sous le choc et une suspecte désormais aux mains de la gendarmerie. Rien ne laissait présager l'issue fatale de cette soirée dans le village de Sam Ndiaye, situé sur l'axe Ndiobène. En début de soirée, Cheikhou Oumar Ndiaye, conducteur de bus de la ligne 10 du réseau urbain de Thiès et cultivateur, regagnait le domicile conjugal après avoir travaillé dans les champs familiaux en compagnie de ses deux épouses. Cependant, une vive altercation a rapidement éclaté au sein du foyer. Asta Dia, sa seconde épouse âgée d'une trentaine d'années et originaire de Mballène, l'accusait d'avoir battu son fils né d'un précédent mariage, une imputation que le chef de famille réfutait catégoriquement. La tension s'est accrue lorsque la présence d'une arme blanche dissimulée par Asta Dia sous son pagne ou sous un oreiller a été repérée. Informée de la menace, la mère du défunt a alerté le frère aîné de Cheikhou Oumar Ndiaye, qui s'est rendu sur place pour sermonner le couple et confisquer le couteau. Pensant la situation apaisée après cette intervention familiale, Cheikhou Oumar Ndiaye s'est endormi sur le dos dans sa chambre. Cependant, la mise en cause, enceinte de son premier enfant avec la victime, est revenue à la charge au cœur de la nuit. Après avoir confié son fils à des voisins, elle s'est procuré un second couteau avant de revenir sur les lieux. Surprenant son époux endormi, elle lui a asséné froidement deux coups de couteau, dont l'un s'est avéré mortel. Grièvement blessé et perdant abondamment son sang, Cheikhou Oumar Ndiaye a réussi à se traîner jusqu'à l'entrée de la concession en criant « Asta raynama » (« Asta m'a tué ») avant de s'écrouler. À la suite de son acte, la suspecte s'est enfuie avec son fils pour se réfugier dans une maison voisine, où elle a été rapidement interpellée par les gendarmes de Fandène. Placée en garde à vue sous la qualification de meurtre aggravé (uxoricide), elle fait l'objet d'une enquête judiciaire sous la direction du parquet compétent. Inhumé le lendemain, le défunt laisse derrière lui six orphelins. Témoignant du passé tumultueux du couple, la sœur du défunt, K. Ndiaye, a rappelé qu'Asta Dia avait déjà brandi une arme blanche lors d'une dispute précédente, avant d'exprimer la douleur de toute une communauté : « Elle n'a pas tué Cheikhou, mais toute une famille ». L’article Drame conjugal a Sénégal : Cheikhou Oumar Ndiaye poignardé à mort dans son sommeil par sa seconde épouse est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Labé : un adolescent de 14 ans grièvement brûlé à Kouroula, un jeune de 18 ans interpellé
items.description: Un apprenti réparateur d’appareils électroniques âgé de 14 ans a été grièvement brûlé vendredi 9 octobre 2026, au quartier Kouroula, dans la commune urbaine de Labé. Selon le maître de la victime, un jeune de 18 ans l’aurait volontairement incendié alors qu’il tentait d’enlever de la peinture sur son corps avec de l’essence. Le suspect a été interpellé par les gendarmes et serait en cours d’audition. Les faits se sont produits dans un atelier de réparation d’appareils électroniques où travaillait Mamadou Saidou Diallo, la jeune victime. L’adolescent aurait été atteint à plusieurs parties du corps, notamment à la tête, à la gorge, à la poitrine et aux bras. Joint au sujet de l’incident, Mamadou Saliou Diallo, maître de l’apprenti, explique que l’adolescent avait reçu de la peinture sur le corps au cours d’une opération de remise en état d’un téléviseur. « On dépannait un poste téléviseur et, au finish, il fallait le revêtir de peinture. C’est dans cette opération que le petit a eu cette peinture sur le corps », a-t-il raconté. Selon son témoignage, la victime cherchait ensuite à enlever la peinture à l’aide d’essence lorsqu’un jeune de 18 ans, identifié sous le prénom de Kaba, aurait acheté des allumettes avant de mettre le feu sur lui. Le maître de la victime affirme qu’aucune altercation n’avait précédé les faits. « Il n’y a pas eu de discussion entre eux, ni rien. Le présumé auteur n’est même pas dans mon atelier. Il était venu jouer au casino et il loge non loin de l’hôpital régional de Labé », a-t-il précisé. La victime prise en charge à l’hôpital régional Après l’incident, Mamadou Saidou Diallo a été évacué au service de traumatologie de l’hôpital régional de Labé pour recevoir des soins. D’après son maître, les médecins se sont montrés rassurants quant à sa prise en charge. Lors d’un échange avec l’adolescent le lendemain des faits, celui-ci était conscient. « Les médecins l’ont traité et ils m’ont dit être en mesure de le soigner convenablement. Ce matin, j’ai échangé avec lui et il est conscient », a indiqué Mamadou Saliou Diallo. Le suspect interpellé par les gendarmes Concernant le jeune mis en cause, le maître de la victime affirme que celui-ci aurait envisagé de rentrer chez lui après l’hospitalisation de l’adolescent. Il aurait finalement été interpellé par les gendarmes. « C’est entre-temps que les gendarmes l’ont interpellé. Il est actuellement en audition afin de déterminer ce qui l’a poussé à commettre cet acte », a-t-il ajouté. Pour l’heure, les circonstances précises de cet incident ainsi que les motivations du geste présumé restent à établir par les services compétents. Le jeune de 18 ans est présumé innocent jusqu’à l’établissement éventuel de sa culpabilité par la justice. Alpha Moussa Dieng, correspondant régional à Labé L’article Labé : un adolescent de 14 ans grièvement brûlé à Kouroula, un jeune de 18 ans interpellé est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: US releases fresh names, photos of 24 Nigerians to be deported
items.description: The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has published the names and photographs of 24 Nigerians arrested by immigration authorities in connection with various criminal offences, as the country continues its deportation operations. The individuals were arrested in different parts of the United States by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), according to information released by DHS. The offences listed against them range from wire and mail fraud to money laundering, drug-related crimes, identity theft, assault, forgery and cruelty towards a child. In a statement announcing the arrests, DHS said the publication was intended to highlight non-US citizens with criminal records who had been apprehended by immigration enforcement officers. “The U.S. Department of Homeland Security is highlighting the worst of worst criminal aliens arrested by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE),” the department said. It added: “Under DHS leadership, the hardworking men and women of DHS and ICE are fulfilling President Trump’s promise and carrying out mass deportations – starting with the worst of the worst – including the illegal aliens you see here.” Full list of 24 Nigerians named by US authorities The list released by DHS identifies the Nigerian nationals, the offences associated with their arrests and the locations where they were apprehended. 1. Emmanuel Omowaiye Offence: Mail fraud Arrest location: Richmond, Texas 2. Laurene Onwuka Offences: Fraud and impersonation Arrest location: Chantilly, Virginia 3. Olusegun Shonekan Offence: Wire fraud Arrest location: Newark, New Jersey 4. Olusegun Olaseni Offence: Amphetamine sale Arrest location: Greencastle, Indiana 5. Shedrack Umukoro Offence: Money laundering Arrest location: Yazoo City, Mississippi 8. Olasoji Akinbode Offences: Fraud and impersonation Arrest location: Kearny, New Jersey 9. Oluwatosin Afolabi Offence: Fraud Arrest location: Conroe, Texas 10. Alameen Adetunji Tokosi Offence: Drug possession Arrest location: Chicago, Illinois 11. Joshua Ipoade Offence: Wire fraud Arrest location: Atlanta, Georgia 12. Michael Orji Offences: Weapons offence, fraud, identity theft, wire fraud, false citizenship and money laundering Arrest location: Oxford, Wisconsin 13. Ahmadu Apooyin Offence: Drug-related offence Arrest location: Baltimore, Maryland 14. Teslim Kiriji Offence: Money laundering Arrest location: Yazoo City, Mississippi 15. Onomen Uduebor Offence: Identity theft Arrest location: Seattle, Washington 16. Charles Ochi Offence: Money laundering Arrest location: White Deer, Pennsylvania 17. Daniel Eta Offence: Wire fraud Arrest location: White Deer, Pennsylvania 18. Ifeanyi Ibennah Offence: Cruelty towards a child Arrest location: Tampa, Florida 19. Kazeem Runsewe Offence: Wire fraud Arrest location: Thomson, Illinois 20. Fatiu Lawal Offence: Wire fraud Arrest location: Lompoc, California 21. Justin Akubueze Offence: Money laundering Arrest location: Orem, Utah 22. Moyinoluwaseun Okeowo Offences: Larceny, forgery and concealing stolen property Arrest location: Orlando, Florida 23. Babajide Oluwaseun Faseyi Offence: Assault Arrest location: Alden, New York 24. Bright Eigbedion Offence: Money laundering Arrest location: Lompoc, California DHS said the publication was part of the government’s wider immigration enforcement campaign, with ICE responsible for carrying out arrests across the country. The announcement comes amid continued efforts by the US administration to remove non-citizens considered priorities for immigration enforcement. However, the DHS announcement does not provide detailed information about the final immigration status or deportation proceedings of each individual. Being named on the list should therefore not, by itself, be taken as confirmation that a person has already been deported. items.title: Kagbélen : le budget communal réduit de 8 milliards GNF, un conseiller dénonce des irrégularités
items.description: Le budget de la commune urbaine de Kagbélen est passé de 25 à 17 milliards de francs guinéens après une révision opérée par le nouvel exécutif communal. Si le maire met en avant la nécessité d’adapter les prévisions aux priorités de son équipe, le conseiller communal Karim Bailo Barry dénonce des manquements présumés dans l’organisation de la session budgétaire du 8 octobre 2026, notamment l’absence de convocation officielle et la transmission tardive des documents. La révision du budget communal et les conditions de son examen suscitent des interrogations à Kagbélen. Présenté lors de la session budgétaire du 8 octobre 2026, le budget est désormais arrêté à 17 milliards de francs guinéens, contre 25 milliards initialement prévus. À l’ouverture des travaux, le député élu de Kagbélen, Mohamed Cissé, a rappelé cette baisse des prévisions financières, tout en insistant sur la nécessité de mobiliser les ressources nécessaires à la réalisation des investissements annoncés. « Le plus important est que ce montant-là soit mobilisé, que les investissements qui sont prévus pour la commune de Kagbélen se fassent d’ici le 31 décembre 2026 », a-t-il déclaré. Le député a également attiré l’attention sur les besoins de la commune en matière de routes, d’accès à l’eau potable et d’infrastructures scolaires. Selon les chiffres qu’il a avancés, sur les 310 écoles recensées à Kagbélen, seules 19 appartiennent à l’État. Il a ainsi invité les autorités communales à explorer les possibilités de financement auprès de partenaires. « Il faudrait qu’ils trouvent les fonds. Ils ont tous les moyens et toutes les opportunités de chercher les fonds un peu partout », a-t-il recommandé. Le maire justifie la révision budgétaire Pour le maire de Kagbélen, Sona Mady Doumbouya, la révision du budget répond à la nécessité d’adapter les prévisions héritées de la délégation spéciale aux orientations de la nouvelle équipe communale. « Nous venons d’être élus, on a trouvé un budget en place qui était conçu par la délégation spéciale, alors que nous n’avons pas les mêmes objectifs, même programme, même feuille de route. Donc, pour adapter à notre réalité, c’est pourquoi on a décidé de remanier pour pouvoir mener nos activités d’ici fin de l’année », a-t-il expliqué. Parmi les projets évoqués figurent l’entretien du pont de Kagbélen, la construction d’un centre de santé à Bailobaya, la réalisation de forages et la construction d’écoles, en fonction des ressources disponibles. Le maire s’est par ailleurs félicité de la participation des conseillers à cette session, affirmant que 43 des 45 membres du conseil communal étaient présents. Karim Bailo Barry conteste la procédure Mais au-delà du contenu du budget, le conseiller communal Karim Bailo Barry soulève des préoccupations concernant les conditions dans lesquelles la session s’est tenue. Il affirme que plusieurs conseillers n’ont pas reçu de convocation officielle et n’ont pu consulter les documents budgétaires qu’une fois arrivés dans la salle de réunion. « En effet, lors de la session budgétaire du 8 octobre 2026, nous affirmons n’avoir reçu aucune convocation officielle et n’avoir obtenu les documents relatifs au projet de budget qu’une fois dans la salle de séance », dénonce-t-il. Le conseiller estime que ces faits soulèvent des questions quant au respect des dispositions des articles 113 et 114, qu’il invoque au sujet des délais de convocation et de la communication préalable des documents nécessaires aux délibérations. Il rappelle également qu’une saisine collective a été adressée à l’autorité de tutelle le 24 août 2026, sous le numéro 2256, afin de solliciter un contrôle de légalité et de conformité aux textes en vigueur. « Pourtant, à ce jour, nous n’avons reçu aucune notification nous informant des suites réservées à cette saisine », affirme-t-il. Karim Bailo Barry demande ainsi à l’autorité de tutelle d’examiner les faits signalés, de vérifier la régularité des procédures et d’informer les conseillers des suites données à leur démarche. Il tient toutefois à préciser que sa contestation ne vise pas à paralyser le fonctionnement de la mairie. « Notre objectif n’est ni de bloquer l’administration communale ni d’entraver le processus budgétaire. Il est de veiller à ce que les décisions engageant l’avenir de nos citoyens soient prises dans des conditions régulières, transparentes et conformes à la loi », souligne-t-il. Le conseiller conclut en rappelant l’importance de la transparence dans la gestion des affaires publiques locales. « La transparence n’est pas une faveur accordée aux conseillers : elle est une exigence de bonne gouvernance et un droit que nous avons le devoir de défendre au nom des citoyens de Kagbélen », affirme-t-il. Entre les ambitions d’investissement affichées par le nouvel exécutif et les contestations soulevées autour de la procédure budgétaire, la commune de Kagbélen devra désormais conjuguer mobilisation des ressources, réalisation des projets et respect des règles de fonctionnement du conseil communal. Les manquements dénoncés par Karim Bailo Barry demeurent, à ce stade, des allégations qui nécessitent un examen par les autorités compétentes. items.title: 2027 will be Atiku’s easiest election; hungry Nigerians will vote for him — Shaibu
items.description: Phrank Shaibu, a communication aide to former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, has said the 2027 presidential election will be the easiest for his principal, predicting that Nigerians struggling with economic hardship will vote for him. Shaibu said Atiku would gain additional votes from Nigerians dissatisfied with the economic conditions under President Bola Tinubu’s administration. He stated this during an interview on the Mic On Podcast while responding to a question about how Atiku could improve on his performance in the 2023 presidential election, when he secured 29 per cent of the votes, amid Tinubu’s incumbency and political structure. “The pathway is simple, and this one, it’s going to be one of the easiest elections for Atiku Abubakar,” Shaibu said. He argued that hunger and poverty would influence voters’ decisions in 2027, expressing confidence that Nigerians seeking relief from economic hardship would support the former vice-president. “Hungry Nigerians, impoverished Nigerians, who are excited that life will be affordable again, will vote Atiku massively come January 16,” he said. Shaibu insisted that Atiku’s expected votes would come from Nigerians who believe the current administration had failed to improve their living conditions. He also claimed that Tinubu and members of his family and cabinet were aware of the administration’s shortcomings. “Tinubu is aware himself that he has failed. His wife is aware that he has failed. His son is aware that he has failed. His ministers are aware that he has failed,” Shaibu said. The aide also questioned the need for the government to engage thousands of social media influencers to publicise its achievements. He was reacting to recent remarks by the Minister of Works, David Umahi, about plans to engage 4,000 influencers to showcase the administration’s projects. Shaibu argued that a government that had made a significant impact on citizens’ lives should be able to demonstrate its achievements without relying heavily on influencers. “That was why Umahi was on TV the other day, and he told the whole world how he is going to hire 4,000 influencers to showcase what they have done,” he said. “Influencing means you need to make believe. You need to show people. You don’t need to struggle to show what you have done if you have made impact in the last three and a half years.” The post 2027 will be Atiku’s easiest election; hungry Nigerians will vote for him — Shaibu appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Assainissement : le contrat de réhabilitation de la décharge de Dar-Es-Salam signé, les travaux annoncés en novembre
items.description: La réhabilitation de la décharge de Dar-Es-Salam, dans la commune de Gbessia, franchit une nouvelle étape. Le contrat relatif aux travaux a été signé entre les ministères concernés, avec un démarrage prévu au cours de la première semaine de novembre 2026, selon la Cellule de communication du ministère de l’Assainissement, de l’Hydraulique et des Hydrocarbures. Le projet de réhabilitation et d’aménagement de la décharge de Dar-Es-Salam entre dans une nouvelle phase. Le ministère de l’Assainissement, de l’Hydraulique et des Hydrocarbures (MAHH) et le ministère de l’Économie, des Finances et du Budget ont procédé à la signature du contrat encadrant la réalisation des travaux, rapporte la Cellule de communication du MAHH. Présidant la cérémonie, le responsable du département a souligné l’importance d’une mobilisation collective pour mener à bien ce projet destiné à améliorer la gestion des déchets et les conditions de vie des populations riveraines. Il a également insisté sur le respect des délais contractuels et la rigueur dans l’exécution des travaux. De son côté, le Gouvernement s’est engagé à honorer ses obligations dans les délais convenus afin de garantir le bon déroulement du chantier. Selon la Cellule de communication du ministère, le lancement des travaux est prévu durant la première semaine de novembre 2026. À terme, cette opération ambitionne de réduire les nuisances et les risques liés à la proximité de la décharge, tout en faisant de Dar-Es-Salam un espace réaménagé et attractif. Le projet s’inscrit dans la dynamique de modernisation des villes et d’amélioration du cadre de vie des populations, dans le cadre du programme Simandou 2040 porté par les autorités guinéennes. items.title: Timeline: A concise history of emergency rule in Pakistan
items.description: The federal government on Sunday imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa following the president’s approval of the recommendations by the federal cabinet. The measures have been approved under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, the President House said in a statement. The two provisions pertain to the proclamation of emergency and governor’s rule. Article 232 of the Constitution deals with “proclamation of emergency on account of war and internal disturbance”, while Article 234 of the Constitution, more commonly known as “governor’s rule”, empowers the federal government to take control of a province in case of “failure of constitutional machinery”. This isn’t the first time the Centre has used its powers to declare emergency in a province or even send the respective provincial government packing. Here’s a brief history of emergency rule in Pakistan. January 1949 to April 1951 The first governor’s rule was imposed within a short span of the country’s establishment, in the heartland of Punjab. In January 1949, then Prime Minister Liaquat Ali Khan visited Lahore, where Chief Minister Nawab Mamdot told him that he had earned the confidence of a majority of the MPAs in the provincial assembly. The development had come about due to a disagreement between Mamdot and former CM Mumtaz Daulatana. However, Liaquat Ali Khan noted factual discrepancies in the document shown by Mamdot. He dismissed the Mamdot government, dissolved the assembly, and imposed governor’s rule in the province. December 1951 to May 1953 — Sindh A governor’s rule of 1 year and 144 days lasted in Sindh after Chief Minister Muhammad Ayub Khuhro was dismissed amid allegations of corruption and maladministration. Mian Aminuddin administered the province directly under Governor’s rule, which ended following the 1953 provincial elections, after which Pirzada Abdus Sattar of the Pakistan Muslim League took over. February-April, 1973 — Balochistan On February 14, 1973, Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto dismissed the Balochistan provincial government led by Chief Minister Sardar Attaullah Mengal and removed Governor Mir Ghaus Bakhsh Bizenjo, citing alleged involvement in unrest and the discovery of weapons at the Iraqi embassy in Islamabad. The next day, Nawab Akbar Khan Bugti was appointed as the new Governor of Balochistan, and direct central/governor’s rule was enforced. The federal government also subsequently deployed the Pakistan Army under General Tikka Khan to conduct operations in the mountainous and tribal regions, particularly targeting areas like Lasbela and Marri. The governor’s rule ended in late April the same year, paving the way for Jam Ghulam Qadir Khan to form a new provincial ministry. February-May 1975 — Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor’s rule was imposed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (then known as the North-West Frontier Province) from February 16, 1975, to May 3, 1975, for a total duration of 76 days under Article 232 of the 1973 Constitution due to an emergency. Officials had cited external disruptions beyond local control. At the time, the federal government under PM Bhutto had directed the governor to assume all government powers, ending the cabinet of Chief Minister Sardar Inayatullah Khan Gandapur. The province was overseen by Major General (R) Syed Ghawas until direct rule concluded on May 3, 1975, with Nasrullah Khan Khattak assuming the office of Chief Minister. June-August 1988 — Sindh The second instance of a governor’s rule in Sindh’s history lasted 68 days, from June 24, 1988, to August 31, 1988. The caretaker government of Chief Minister Akhtar Ali Ghulam Qazi of the Islami Jamhoori Ittehad was dismissed. Qazi was replaced by Pakistan Army’s four-star general Rahimuddin Khan as governor. This development came closely after President General Zia-ul-Haq’s nationwide dissolution of Prime Minister Mohammad Khan Junejo’s federal government and all provincial assemblies on May 29, 1988. February-April 1994 — Khyber Pakhtunkhwa One of the country’s most controversial political episodes, the governor’s rule imposed in KP from February 25, 1994 to April 24, 1994 came after Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto suspended the PML-N ministry in the province, led by Sabir Shah. Executive authority was temporarily transferred directly to the provincial Governor, Major General (Retd) Khurshid Ali Khan. When the governor’s rule was lifted, Aftab Ahmad Khan Sherpao of the PPP was sworn in as the new chief minister of the province February-March 2009 — Punjab President Asif Ali Zardari imposed governor’s rule for two months, dismissing PML-N’s government after the Supreme Court disqualified Nawaz Sharif and Shehbaz Sharif. Zardari appointed Salman Taseer as the governor of Punjab. The provincial assembly was not suspended, but then-CM Shehbaz and his cabinet members were barred from holding office. The governor’s rule was lifted after a month. January-March 2013 — Balochistan PPP’s Prime Minister Raja Pervez Ashraf dismissed Balochistan’s provincial government, yielding to nationwide protests. His announcement came as thousands of Hazara Shias staged a sit-in in freezing cold on Alamdar Road for three days, along with the bodies of dozens of people killed in twin bombings in Quetta The carnage had resulted in over 90 fatalities. The provincial government of Chief Minister Nawab Aslam Raisani was sacked, and Governor Nawab Zulfiqar Ali Magsi took charge as the chief executive of the province. Nationwide emergencies Nationwide emergencies have been imposed several times as well, including martial laws, with the first one just a few years after Pakistan’s creation, in 1954. The longest periods in the country’s history when a nationwide dismissal of parliament persisted were in the martial laws of 1977–1985 under General Zia-ul-Haq, and 1999–2007 under General Pervez Musharraf. Timeline of emergency proclamations Oct 1954 Governor General Ghulam Mohammad proclaims emergency. Oct 1958 President Iskander Mirza abrogates the 1956 Constitution under emergency rule. Gen Ayub is appointed as chief martial law administrator (CMLA). Mar 1969 Gen Ayub passes presidency to Gen Yahya, who abrogates the 1962 Constitution under proclamation of emergency and becomes CMLA. Dec 1971 Zulfikar Ali Bhutto succeeds Gen Yahya as the next CMLA. July 1977 Gen Zia takes over as CMLA and holds the 1973 Constitution in abeyance under emergency rule. Aug 1990 President Ghulam Ishaq Khan declares a state of emergency after dismissing the government of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto. May 1998 A constitutional emergency is imposed after Pakistan conducts nuclear tests. Oct 1999 Nov 2007 Gen Musharraf imposes a state of emergency and holds the 1973 Constitution in abeyance. items.title: Soldier martyred, 12 terrorists killed as security forces foil infiltration attempt in Kurram: ISPR
items.description: A soldier was martyred and 12 terrorists killed in an exchange of fire in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Kurram district, the army’s media wing said on Sunday. The Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said that the movement of a group of khawarij attempting to cross the international border from Afghanistan into Pakistan was detected in Kurram district on Sunday, where security forces engaged them effectively. Fitna al Khawarij is a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan. Security forces, “maintaining a high state of alertness and vigilance, effectively thwarted the infiltration attempt”, the statement added. It further said that Afghan Taliban posts had also opened fire to support the infiltration attempt by the khawarij. “The skilful and precise engagement by vigilant troops resulted in the killing of 12 khawarij and Afghan Taliban,” the statement said. During the exchange of fire, Naib Subedar Hidayat Aman was martyred after “fighting gallantly”. This incident along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border vindicates Islamabad’s “objective and factual stance regarding the willful abject failure of the Afghan Taliban regime to deny the use of Afghan soil to the terrorist organisation”, the statement added. “The security forces of Pakistan remain resolute and unwavering in their commitment to defend the nation’s frontiers,” said the ISPR, adding that sanitisation operation is being conducted in the area to eliminate any other Indian sponsored khawariji found in the area.” “The relentless counter-terrorism campaign under vision Azm-i-Istehkam as approved by Federal Apex Committee on National Action Plan by security forces and law enforcement agencies of Pakistan will continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign sponsored and supported terrorism from the country.” “These sacrifices of our brave soldiers further reinforce our unwavering commitment to safeguarding our nation and its frontiers at all costs,” it said. In a statement on X, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi paid tribute to the security forces for “foiling the infiltration attempt”. He expressed “heartfelt condolences and expression of sympathy” to the bereaved family of the martyred Naib Subedar Hidayat Aman, adding that nation takes pride in the “professional capabilities and courage” of the security forces. KP has been witnessing terrorist attacks and security challenges for a long time September particularly witnessed a significant deterioration in Pakistan’s overall security environment, accompanied by growing political, economic and regional pressures, according to Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS) . Terrorist violence increased substantially , with 225 attacks recorded nationwide, compared with 199 in August, representing a 13.1 per cent increase and the highest monthly total recorded in 12 years. On Sept 27 , 14 people, including two rescue officials, were martyred and 35 sustained injuries after a suicide bomber rammed an explosive-laden vehicle into a police checkpost in and then targeted an ambulance taking bodies to hospital in DI Khan. On Sept 18, a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation .
